title: What that adoration really is is clearest from Rome’s solemn universal temple-practice, approved or silently allowed by pastors and Pope
source_text: XVI. Verum quae & qualis sit illa adoratio quae, juxta mentem Ecclesiae Romanae, imaginibus Christi & Sanctorum debetur, certius colligi non potest quam ex istius Ecclesiae praxi solenni & universali. Hoc autem nomine merito donandus est cultus ille, qui in templis Ecclesiae Romanae imaginibus palam exhibetur, scientibus & videntibus omnibus, ac per solennes quasdam & publicas ceremonias, in quibus plebs Romana pietatis suae partem constituit; non repugnantibus, nec improbantibus Pastoribus ordinariis, nec Episcopis, neque Papa; sed contra cum multorum Doctorum & Episcoporum expressa approbatione, & aliorum tacito consensu; quandoquidem ea de re silent, neque quicquam contra proferunt.
pass_a_gloss: But what and of what sort that adoration is which, according to the mind of the Roman Church, is owed to the images of Christ and of the Saints, cannot be more certainly gathered than from that Church’s solemn and universal practice. But under this name that cult is deservedly to be counted which in the temples of the Roman Church is openly exhibited to images, with all knowing and seeing, and through certain solemn and public ceremonies in which the Roman people constitutes a part of its piety; the ordinary Pastors not resisting nor disapproving, nor the Bishops, nor the Pope; but on the contrary with the express approval of many Doctors and Bishops, and the tacit consent of others; since they are silent on the matter and bring forward nothing against it.
pass_b_english: Rome’s real image-adoration is best read from her public temple practice.
Bishops, pastors, and Pope either approve or stay silent while the people make it part of piety.

choices.why: Public, not merely private, cult fixes the doctrine’s meaning.
